title: Public, private, static, dynamic — and what actually breaks
summary: The address types you will be asked about, what RFC 1918 is really for, and why 'static vs dynamic' is an operational choice rather than a technical one.

sections.heading: Private addressing exists because IPv4 ran out
sections.html:
RFC 1918 reserved three ranges that are never routed on the public internet:

RangeSizeTypical use
10.0.0.0/816.7MEnterprise, cloud VPCs
172.16.0.0/121MEnterprises, container networks
192.168.0.0/1665kHome and small offices

They are reusable because every organisation can use the same numbers internally; NAT at the edge translates to a public address. The important interview point is the consequence: two hosts in different organisations can both be 10.0.0.5, so private addresses are meaningless without context. That is why 'can you ping 10.0.0.5?' is not a complete question.

Other special ranges worth knowing:

  • 169.254.0.0/16 — link-local (APIPA on Windows). Seeing this on a Linux host usually means DHCP failed.
  • 127.0.0.0/8 — loopback. 127.0.0.1 never leaves the host.
  • 0.0.0.0/8 — 'this host / any address'. A default route is 0.0.0.0/0.
  • 224.0.0.0/4 — multicast; 255.255.255.255 — limited broadcast.

sections.heading: Static vs dynamic is a policy decision
sections.html:
Both give a host an address, mask, gateway and DNS. The difference is who decides and what happens when the network changes:

StaticDynamic (DHCP)
Change managementManual per host, drift over timeCentral scope, one place to change
Failure modeTypo, duplicate address, stale gatewayServer unreachable, exhausted pool, wrong options
Good forRouters, servers, printers, anything DNS points atClients, laptops, VMs, phones, anything that moves

In practice you see both: a DHCP reservation gives a stable address while keeping central management. That detail often earns credit in an interview because it shows you have operated a real network rather than a textbook one.

sections.heading: Duplicate addresses and conflicts
sections.html:
When two hosts claim the same IPv4 address, behaviour is ugly and non-deterministic: ARP replies race, the switch's MAC table flaps between two ports, connections die mid-transfer, and monitoring shows an address that 'sometimes' responds. Modern Linux uses Address Conflict Detection (ACD) for statically assigned addresses via ip addr add ... with arping-style probing, and systemd-networkd logs 'DuplicateAddressDetection' failures. DHCP servers commonly probe with ARP before offering a lease.

Practical detection: arping -D -I eth0 10.0.0.5 asks 'does anyone else own this address?' without configuring it. On a switch you can look for the same MAC appearing on two ports, or the same IP in two ARP entries.

checks.prompt: A Linux laptop shows address 169.254.23.11/16 and no default route. What is the most likely cause?
options: DHCP did not complete, so the kernel self-assigned a link-local address
checks.explanation: 169.254.0.0/16 is the IPv4 link-local range used when no DHCP lease is obtained. It implies L2 connectivity may exist but configuration did not arrive.

why_wrong.1: Link-local assignment requires a working interface, so the NIC is at least partly functional.
why_wrong.0: DNS problems do not affect address assignment.
why_wrong.3: The mask is consistent with the self-assigned address; there was no configured mask to get wrong.

checks.prompt: Why do infrastructure servers usually get static addresses or DHCP reservations rather than plain dynamic leases?

checklist.text: DNS records, firewall rules, monitoring and other systems reference the address or name; it must be stable.
A changing address breaks long-lived connections, ACLs and allow-lists.
Reservations keep central management and auditability while guaranteeing stability.
Dynamic leases are fine for clients where address churn is harmless.

checks.reference: Servers are referenced by address and name from many places: DNS A/PTR records, firewall allow-lists, monitoring targets, backup jobs, TLS certificates in some cases, and client configuration. A lease change silently invalidates all of those. Static configuration or a DHCP reservation makes the address part of the contract. Reservations are usually preferred operationally because the scope stays the single source of truth and the server still receives options centrally.

connect.title: DHCP
connect.text: Link-local addressing is DHCP's fallback. The absence of a lease is itself diagnostic evidence.

connect.title: DNS
connect.text: Static addressing is what makes DNS records meaningful for servers; reverse records in particular.

connect.title: NAT
connect.text: Private addressing only works end to end because of translation at the edge — and that breaks inbound connections unless you configure it.

interview.q: What is the difference between a private and a public IP address?
interview.a: Private ranges (RFC 1918) are not routed on the internet and are reused by every organisation; they require NAT or a proxy at the edge to reach public destinations. Public addresses are globally unique and routable. The practical consequence is that private addresses only have meaning in the context of a specific network.

interview.q: You see 169.254.x.x on a host. What do you check?
interview.a: That it is link-local, meaning no DHCP lease. Then: link status, DHCP server reachability (is the server on this L2 segment or is the relay configured), scope exhaustion, and whether the interface is in a network namespace or VLAN without DHCP.
